flashcards.q: Name the non-negotiable tier of the Python quant stack.
flashcards.a: NumPy, SciPy, Statsmodels, QuantLib, cvxpy — the numerical foundation, optimization/root-finding, econometrics, pricing infrastructure, and convex optimization. Everything else is desk-dependent.

flashcards.q: What is QuantLib's object graph for pricing a vanilla option?
flashcards.a: Quote (spot handle) + YieldTermStructure (curve) + BlackVolTermStructure (vol/surface) -> BlackScholesMertonProcess -> EuropeanOption (payoff + exercise) -> attach AnalyticEuropeanEngine -> NPV/delta/gamma/vega/theta. You compose objects; you never call price(option).

flashcards.q: What are the three classic QuantLib gotchas?
flashcards.a: 1) Day counts/calendars (Actual365 vs Thirty360 changes the price), 2) the GLOBAL evaluation date (Settings.instance().evaluationDate — set it explicitly or lose reproducibility), 3) Handles are relinkable references (QuoteHandle/YieldTermCurveHandle) — rebuild a curve without rebuilding the instrument graph.

flashcards.q: Why cvxpy over scipy.optimize.minimize for constrained allocation?
flashcards.a: DCP (disciplined convex programming) VERIFIES convexity before solving — a non-PSD covariance raises an error instead of returning garbage. SLSQP with penalty constraints is fragile, doesn't verify optimality, and fails silently on infeasibility. cvxpy problems also read as math: Problem(Minimize(quad_form(w, S)), [sum(w)==1, w>=0]).

flashcards.q: How do you extract implied vol from a market price?
flashcards.a: Invert BS: brentq (bracketed root-find on [0.01, 3]) over BS(vol) - market_price, or Newton with vega as derivative. Deep ITM/OTM: price-vol curve is nearly flat -> inversion unstable; that IS the smile near expiry. QuantLib has this built in.

flashcards.q: GARCH: which library, what does the fit return, and what is the persistence check?
flashcards.a: arch: arch_model(r, vol='GARCH', p=1, q=1, dist='t').fit() -> the conditional-volatility path (one sigma per day) + params. alpha+beta near 1 = IGARCH territory (persistence shock). EGARCH for the leverage effect (bad news hits harder). Rolling std is a window statistic, NOT a conditional-variance model.

flashcards.q: What is the Statsmodels vs arch division of labor?
flashcards.a: Statsmodels owns the conditional MEAN (OLS, ARIMA/SARIMAX, ADF, Ljung-Box diagnostics); arch owns the conditional VARIANCE (GARCH family, HAR, realized vol) with proper likelihoods. The pair is the standard econometrics workflow — knowing the split is itself a quiz question.

flashcards.q: Your Monte Carlo is slow — the correct order of operations?
flashcards.a: 1) Vectorize (array-shaped simulation, ~1000x on plain paths), 2) Numba @njit(parallel=True, cache=True) for path-dependent logic (~100-500x more), 3) GPU/JAX batch for homogeneous paths. Anti-pattern: Numba BEFORE vectorizing. Multiprocessing ignores the 1000x sitting in array shape.

flashcards.q: What is the modern RNG discipline and the modern way to get Greeks?
flashcards.a: RNG: np.random.Generator(np.random.PCG64(seed)) — explicit object, never the global legacy np.random.seed. Greeks: autodiff — JAX grad through the pricing graph, one pass for all Greeks, replacing 4x-paths finite differences.

flashcards.q: What problem does Black-Litterman solve, and what does it collapse to with no views?
flashcards.a: MVO's INPUTS (mu especially) carry huge estimation error; the optimizer amplifies it (max-Sharpe weights jump on resampling). BL fixes the input: market-implied prior (reverse optimization from cap weights) blended with views tuned by confidence Omega. No views -> collapses to the market prior. It's a better ESTIMATOR, not a better solver.

flashcards.q: Why does max-Sharpe allocation need shrinkage (Ledoit-Wolf)?
flashcards.a: Sample covariance at typical N << T is badly conditioned — even non-PSD; the optimizer (an error amplifier) turns input noise into extreme weights. Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage (or nearest-PSD projection, or a factor model) stabilizes S. sklearn.covariance.LedoitWolf is a two-line fix.

The ALLOCATION step only: EfficientFrontier (max_sharpe/min_volatility/efficient_return) + Black-Litterman + HRP. Estimating mu and S remains YOUR problem. HRP (hierarchical risk parity) survives ill-conditioned covariances because it needs no matrix inversion.

flashcards.q: What is TA-Lib's role and its definitional trap?
flashcards.a: 150+ C-speed indicator functions behind a uniform API; institutional role is signal computation in backtests, not chart decoration. Trap: TA-Lib's RSI uses WILDER's smoothing (recursive alpha=1/n), not SMA-of-changes — convention mismatch is the first debug in any 'my signals don't match the platform' incident.

flashcards.q: pandas vs polars for market data?
flashcards.a: pandas: the desk lingua franca, ecosystem, ergonomics — daily bars and option chains fit. polars/pyarrow: multi-GB tick panels at 10-100x via columnar engine. Production cut is literal data size; both join at parquet. yfinance is prototype tier — production is the firm's market-data platform.

flashcards.q: Reconcile 'learn the math, not the libraries' with a whole module on libraries.
flashcards.a: The libraries encode the math's OPERATIONAL layer (day counts, likelihoods, solvers); QuantLib without Black-Scholes is a technician, Black-Scholes without a curve builder can't produce a price. The mistake is libraries INSTEAD of mathematics — the tier list sequences, it doesn't replace. Interviews test derivations first because they're the scarce, hard-to-train signal.
